extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners (PRSA members and communications professionals)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and position guidance from PRSA's Board of Ethics and Professional Standards (BEPS) describing ethical requirements and recommended practices for public relations activities across media, social platforms, influencers, billing, and disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and scope of the PRSA Code of Ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: The PRSA Code of Ethics exists to inspire ethical behavior, clearly identify improper public relations practices and teach members how to avoid them. It applies to PRSA members and sets out principles that uphold core values including advocacy, honesty, expertise, independence, loyalty and fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a voluntary organization PRSA establishes voluntary practice standards, codes of conduct and practice guidelines, inspires and educates best practice, promotes voluntary compliance, and defines what is unethical or improper (threats to ethical practice; behaviors inconsistent with the Code; disruptive behaviors; practices destructive to the reputation of practitioners, the profession, or PRSA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of BEPS (Board of Ethics and Professional Standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: BEPS is comprised of senior professionals and PRSA members created to recognize and acknowledge ethical issues, provide educational resources and training, and uphold and amend the PRSA Code of Ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BEPS provides case studies, position papers, blogs and other assets; it also publishes a BEPS Handbook and an Application to contact BEPS. For inquiries or to inform BEPS about a concern, members may email beps@prsa.org or complete the form; allow three weeks before re-contacting BEPS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of PRSA enforcement authority
rubrics_metrics.description: PRSA is a voluntary organization and its enforcement authority is limited; it cannot impose government-style sanctions or licensing actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations with enforceable regulations derive power from legislation or government authority; PRSA does not, and therefore focuses on establishing aspirational and voluntary standards rather than statutory enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay-for-play (position and prohibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay-for-play occurs when payment is required for the development and publishing of content (blog posts, videos, interviews, columns, etc.) and such payments are undisclosed, creating a quid pro quo that can deceive consumers into believing content was selected on merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BEPS states pay-for-play conflicts with several PRSA Code provisions and professional values. It specifically cites violations of Free Flow of Information, Disclosure of Information, Conflicts of Interest, and Enhancing the Profession. Recommendations: request and include disclosure with the final information product when compensation was provided; encourage disclosure of travel, lodging, gifts or non-monetary compensation; always encourage clear and obvious disclosure of material information consumers should reasonably expect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical use of social media
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations practitioners must incorporate a higher standard of practice by adhering to the PRSA Code of Ethics in all applications of social media strategies, tactics and utilization, recognizing the speed, reach, and unregulated nature of social platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four Code provisions are highlighted for social media: Disclosure of Information (fully disclose paid placements and associations), Safeguarding Confidences (protect confidential/private information), Conflicts of Interest (disclose conflicts and require influencer disclosures per FTC guidelines), and Enhancing the Profession. Practical points: recognize interdependency between news orgs and social media, require disclosures for paid placements and gifts (nominal, legal, infrequent), be aware of employee free speech rights under NLRB, and treat trust as the 'ultimate currency' on social platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism (definition and prohibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plagiarism is the unauthorized use or close imitation of another's language and thoughts and representing that content as your own; it can be intentional or inadvertent but carries equal weight in BEPS's view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRSA links plagiarism to Code provisions (Free Flow of Information, Competition, Disclosure of Information, Conflicts of Interest) and values (Honesty, Expertise, Fairness). Recommendations to avoid plagiarism: do not copy another's content even if editing; use your own words and paraphrase; give proper credit when paraphrasing; use quotation marks and credit the source for exact wording; disclose all sources; understand that copyright permission does not absolve the need for attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paid spokespersons and influencers (disclosure and conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone who is paid to serve as a spokesperson, advocate or influencer must disclose the contractual arrangement or relationship between the spokesperson and the compensating interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three Code provisions apply: Disclosure of Information, Conflicts of Interest, and Enhancing the Profession. Recommendations: disclose commercial relationships in advance of or simultaneous to the public forum; every party in the contractual relationship must disclose; be honest and accurate in revealing sponsors and any financial interest; ensure gifts are nominal, legal and infrequent; require influencers and recipients of product samples to make FTC-required disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front groups (deceptive organizations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A front group is an organization created or labeled to mislead the public about its true mission; assisting or creating front groups to hide sponsorships or intent is considered deceptive and a violation of the Code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BEPS's position: any effort to deceive the public is a clear violation of the PRSA Code of Ethics. Four Code provisions are implicated (Free Flow of Information; Disclosure of Information; Conflicts of Interest; Enhancing the Profession). Recommendation: avoid assisting front groups or undisclosed sponsorships even if activities are lawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overstating fees or compensation (billing honesty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Members must charge clients only for services rendered and in accordance with existing contracts; overstating fees, charging for unperformed work, or inflating support data is unethical and harms the profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary Code provision: Enhancing the Profession; relevant values: Honesty, Fairness, Loyalty. Recommendations: bill only for services performed and expenses actually incurred; report services rendered, time spent, out-of-pocket charges, and related fees accurately; adhere to a rigid code of conduct and integrity in billing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Native advertising & sponsored content (disclosure and clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a clear distinction between organic content and sponsored/native advertising; the sponsor should be clearly identified so consumers can distinguish paid content from independent content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five Code provisions apply (Disclosure of Information; Free Flow of Information; Competition; Conflicts of Interest; Enhancing the Profession). Recommendations: ensure sponsorship is fully disclosed within the content context and clearly apparent to consumers; disclosures should be appropriate to the medium, easily identified and recognized, and effectively differentiate paid content from organic content; do not attempt to deceive consumers into believing paid content is independent.

rubrics_metrics.name: BEPS Handbook and practical resources
rubrics_metrics.description: BEPS publishes a Handbook that includes the Application to BEPS and supplemental ethics information and tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contents mentioned: The History of BEPs; Eight Ethics Questions to Ask Yourself Before Acting; Six Statements That Should Warn You of a Potential Ethical Violation; Six Indications That Your Company Has an Ethical Culture; Eight Ethics Quotes; Six Practical Recommendations for Building Employer Branding; plus the Application and contact process. Use these resources for training, policy development, and to guide individual ethical decision-making.
